# Linear regression with a single predictor

## Regression model {#regression-model-1}

A regression model separates an observed outcome into a systematic part and an unexplained part:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y &= \text{Model} + \text{Error} \\
  &= f(X) + \epsilon \\
  &= \mu_{Y \mid X} + \epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

- $\mu_{Y \mid X}$ is the mean outcome for observations with predictor value $X$.
- $\epsilon$ is the deviation of an observed outcome from that mean.

## A linear regression model

A linear regression model describes the relationship between a quantitative outcome, $Y$, and a quantitative predictor, $X$:

$$
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon
$$

::: incremental
- $\beta_0$: population intercept
- $\beta_1$: population slope
- $\epsilon$: unexplained deviation from the line
:::

## The fitted regression line

We use data to estimate the population relationship:

$$
\widehat{Y} = b_0 + b_1 X
$$

- $\widehat{Y}$: predicted value of the outcome
- $b_0$: estimated intercept
- $b_1$: estimated slope

::: {.callout-note .fragment .small}
There is **no error term** in the fitted line: $\widehat{Y}$ is the model's prediction, not an observed outcome.
:::

# Example

## Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(fivethirtyeight)
```

## Dataset

-   A dataset of 146 movies, their critic scores, and their audience scores

```{r}
#| label: data-prep
#| echo: false
movie_scores <- fandango |>
  rename(
    critic = rottentomatoes,
    audience = rottentomatoes_user
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: data-overview
movie_scores |>
  select(film, critic, audience)
```

## Goal

Describe the relationship between film critics' scores and audience scores

## Data visualization

```{r}
#| label: scatterplot
ggplot(movie_scores, aes(x = critic, y = audience)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Critic Score", y = "Audience Score")
```

## Visualizing the linear regression model

```{r}
#| label: viz-model
ggplot(movie_scores, aes(x = critic, y = audience)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Critic Score", y = "Audience Score")
```

## Building the model in R

## State the model type

```{r}
linear_reg()
```


## Fit the model

```{r}
linear_reg() |>
  fit(
    audience ~ critic,
    data = movie_scores
  )
```

## Fit the model, and save it

```{r}
movies_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(
    audience ~ critic,
    data = movie_scores
  )
```

## Summarize the model

```{r}
tidy(movies_fit)
```

## Write the model equation {.smaller}

```{r}
tidy(movies_fit)
```

$$ \hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1 X $$
$$\widehat{\text{audience}} = 32.3 + 0.519 \times \text{critic}$$

::: {.callout-tip .fragment}

## Reading the model equation

Predicted audience score is 32.3 plus 0.519 times the critic score.

:::

# Slope and intercept

## Participate {.xsmall}


The slope of the fitted model is 0.519.
Which of the following is the best interpretation of this value?

$$\widehat{\text{audience}} = 32.3 + 0.519 \times \text{critic}$$

a) Increasing the critic score by one point causes the audience score to increase by 0.519 points.
b) For every one point increase in the critic score, the audience score is expected to be higher, on average, by 0.519 points.
c) Audiences tend to rate movies 0.519 points higher, on average, than critics do.
d) For every one point increase in the audience score, the critic score goes up by 0.519 points, on average.

## Participate {.xsmall}


The intercept of the fitted model is 32.3.
Which of the following is the best interpretation of this value?

$$\widehat{\text{audience}} = 32.3 + 0.519 \times \text{critic}$$


a) For movies with a critic score of 0 points, we expect the audience score to be 32.3 points, on average.
b) For movies with an audience score of 0 points, we expect the critic score to be 32.3 points, on average.
c) For every one point increase in the critic score, the audience score goes up by 32.3 points.
d) The average audience scores of movies in the dataset is 32.3.

## Is the intercept meaningful?

The intercept is meaningful in context if:

-   the predictor can feasibly equal or be near zero, and
-   zero is reasonably close to the observed predictor values

. . .

Here, observed critic scores range from `{r} min(movie_scores$critic)` to `{r} max(movie_scores$critic)`.

The intercept is meaningful in context.

# Predictions and residuals

## Make a prediction

Use the linear model to predict the audience score for a movie with a critic
score of 75.

::: incremental
- $\widehat{\text{audience}} = 32.3 + 0.519 \times \text{critic}$

- $\widehat{\text{audience}} = 32.3 + 0.519 \times 75$

- $\widehat{\text{audience}} = 71.225$

- We predict that the audience score will be approximately **71.2**.

:::

## Make a prediction

Use the linear model to predict the audience score for a movie with a critic
score of 75.

$\widehat{\text{audience}} = 71.225$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
m <- lm(audience ~ critic, data = movie_scores)
ggplot(data = movie_scores, mapping = aes(x = critic, y = audience)) +
 geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
 geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#325b74", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
 labs(x = "Critic Score", y = "Audience Score") +
 theme_minimal() +
   annotate(
   "segment",
   x = 75,
   xend = 75,
   y = -Inf,
   yend = 71.225,
   color = "#BE394F"
 ) +
 annotate(
   "segment",
   x = -Inf,
   xend = 75,
   y = 71.225,
   yend = 71.225,
   color = "#BE394F"
 )
```

## Make a prediction with R {.smaller}

- Step 1: Make a new data frame with the predictor value(s) of interest with `tibble()`:

```{r}
new_movie <- tibble(critic = 75)
new_movie
```

::: fragment

- Step 2: Make a prediction for the new dataset using the model with `predict()`:

```{r}
predict(movies_fit, new_data = new_movie)
```

:::

## Residuals

A **residual** is the difference between an observed and predicted outcome:

$$
\text{residual} = \text{observed} - \text{predicted}
= y - \widehat{y}
$$

## Calculating residuals with R {.smaller}

Use `augment()` to add predictions and residuals to the original dataset.

```{r}
movies_aug <- augment(movies_fit, new_data = movie_scores)

movies_aug
```

## Fantastic Four residual

```{r}
movies_aug |>
  select(film, audience, .pred, .resid) |>
  filter(film == "Fantastic Four")
```

## Visualizing a residual

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
ff <- movies_aug |>
  filter(film == "Fantastic Four")

base +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = ff,
    aes(
      xend = critic,
      yend = .pred
    ),
    color = "#9E2C6A",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = ff,
    color = "#9E2C6A",
    size = 3
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = ff$critic + 0.2,
    y = mean(c(ff$audience, ff$.pred)),
    label = "Fantastic Four residual",
    color = "#9E2C6A",
    hjust = 0
  )
```

## Choosing values for $b_0$ and $b_1$

::: question

Which line fits the points best—and what do we mean by “best”?

:::


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
ggplot(movie_scores, aes(x = critic, y = audience)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 32.3155,
    slope = 0.5187,
    color = "#325b74",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 25, slope = 0.7, color = "gray") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 21, slope = 0.9, color = "gray") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 35, slope = 0.3, color = "gray") +
  labs(x = "Critic Score", y = "Audience Score")
```

## Residuals

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

m <- lm(audience ~ critic, data = movie_scores)
ggplot(movie_scores, aes(x = critic, y = audience)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#325b74", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = critic, xend = critic, y = audience, yend = predict(m)),
    color = "steel blue"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Critic Score", y = "Audience Score") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

$$ \text{residual} = \text{observed} - \text{predicted} = y - \hat{y} $$
How far off a predicted value is from the observed (actual) value

## Least squares line {.smaller}

- The residual for the $i^{th}$ observation is

$$
e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i
$$

- Square every residual and add them:

$$
e_1^2 + e_2^2 + \cdots + e_n^2
$$

- The **least squares regression line** is the line that minimizes this sum.

## Properties of least-squares regression {.smaller}

For a least-squares line with one quantitative predictor and an intercept:

::: incremental

- The line passes through the point of means, $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$:
  $$b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}$$

- The slope and correlation have the same sign:
  $$b_1 = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$$

- The residuals sum to zero:
  $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i = 0$$

- The residuals and predictor values are uncorrelated.

:::

# Interpreting responsibly

## Association is not causation {.smaller}

This model tells us that movies with higher critic scores also tend to have higher audience scores.

It does **not** establish that high critic scores cause high audience scores.

## Recap {.xsmall}

::: task
Calculate the predicted body weights of penguins on Biscoe, Dream, and Torgersen islands *by hand*.
:::

$$
\widehat{body~mass} = 4716 - 1003 \times islandDream - 1010 \times islandTorgersen
$$

. . .

-   Biscoe: $\widehat{body~mass} = 4716 - 1003 \times 0 - 1010 \times 0 = 4716$

. . .

-   Dream: $\widehat{body~mass} = 4716 - 1003 \times 1 - 1010 \times 0 = 3713$

. . .

-   Torgersen: $\widehat{body~mass} = 4716 - 1003 \times 0 - 1010 \times 1 = 3706$

## Models with categorical predictors

::: incremental
-   When the categorical predictor has many levels, they're encoded to **dummy variables**.

-   The first level of the categorical variable is the baseline level.
    In a model with one categorical predictor, the intercept is the predicted value of the outcome for the baseline level (x = 0).

-   Each slope coefficient describes the difference between the predicted value of the outcome for that level of the categorical variable compared to the baseline level.
:::
